content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new backdoor attack. The motivation is to find a way to minimize the magnitude of the trigger. This is accomplished by learning a trigger generator. Specifically, the trigger generator function is trained alongside a surrogate victim model in an alternating fashion. The results show that this backdoor attack is more effective than existing methods — both in attack success rate and in accuracy on clean test inputs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
- Missing related work. In particular, the choice of defenses that are used in the experiments in this paper should be expanded on, as there are several defenses missing [1-3]. I think the discussion of alternated training as a treatment for the bilevel optimization problem that data poisoning aims to solve should cover related work, even if they are slightly different in nature (in that they target specific images or classes instead of any image with a trigger) [4, 5].  These prior works are particularly important because they are attacks that require no trigger at all. While historically, we see a division between backdoor attacks that allow for ANY test image with the correct trigger and poisoning attacks that target a particular class or image in the test set, if the goal of this work to hide the trigger in the test input during evaluation, a discussion about that difference should be added. Finally, there are clean-label backdoor attacks not addressed and it would be good to justify why the authors compare to older attacks and not newer ones [6].
    - Defenses worth considering/discussing
        - [1] Paudice, Andrea, et al. "Detection of adversarial training examples in poisoning attacks through anomaly detection." arXiv preprint arXiv:1802.03041 (2018). (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.03041.pdf)
        - [2] Peri, Neehar, et al. "Deep k-nn defense against clean-label data poisoning attacks." European Conference on Computer Vision. Springer, Cham, 2020. (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.13374.pdf)
        - [3] Borgnia, Eitan, et al. "Dp-instahide: Provably defusing poisoning and backdoor attacks with differentially private data augmentations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.02079 (2021).
    - Poisoning attacks that treat the bilevel problem:
        - [4] Huang, W. Ronny, et al. "Metapoison: Practical general-purpose clean-label data poisoning." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 12080-12091.
        - [5] Geiping, Jonas, et al. "Witches' brew: Industrial scale data poisoning via gradient matching." arXiv preprint arXiv:2009.02276 (2020).(https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.02276.pdf)
    - Other clean-label backdoor attacks:
        - [6] Saha, Aniruddha, Akshayvarun Subramanya, and Hamed Pirsiavash. "Hidden trigger backdoor attacks." Proceedings of the AAAI conference on artificial intelligence. Vol. 34. No. 07. 2020.
    - Some of the papers above have not even been cited. Some other papers probably should be cited. I'll point to a couple survey papers here:
        - [7] Ahmed, Ibrahim M., and Manar Younis Kashmoola. "Threats on Machine Learning Technique by Data Poisoning Attack: A Survey." International Conference on Advances in Cyber Security. Springer, Singapore, 2021.
        - [8] Goldblum, Micah, et al. "Dataset security for machine learning: Data poisoning, backdoor attacks, and defenses." IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (2022).
- The experimental setup begs questions.  In another paper that isn't cited here, the sensitivity of poisoning and backdoor attacks  to experimental design is highlighted [9]. Could the author's elaborate a little on the choices of hyperparameters and explain a bit more how this setup isn't favoring their attack? I'm not sure it is... but since there is evidence that these decisions can vastly change the efficacy of data poisoning, I'd like to see a little more discussion on the topic.
    -  [9] Schwarzschild, Avi, et al. "Just how toxic is data poisoning? a unified benchmark for backdoor and data poisoning attacks." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
- It would be nice to see more examples of poisoned images. The appendix has a couple, but I think a larger sample is needed.

Strengths:
- Thorough: lots of datasets, lots of models, lots of other attacks, lots of defenses.
- Well written and clear exposition.
- Nice plots.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality of the writing is good, and the flow of the paper is clear. I think there is novelty in the method, although I'd like to see it better contextualized with other data poisoning attacks, specifically those that involve more direct treatment of the bilevel problem. I did not try to reproduce the work, but I opened the code included in the supplementary material and it seems sufficient. Likewise the information in the paper itself is thorough.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think there is novelty in the method and the results are compelling. Some missing references should be reviewed and considered. I look forward to the discussion with the authors about the points above.

content.title: Thank you for your review, here is our response.
content.comment:
Thank you for your kind comments. We would address your concerns below:  
### 1. More discussion on related works:  
Thanks for for helpful comment. We did not include the papers [1-5] in the original submission since they are about trigger-less data poisoning attacks, which are quite different from backdoor attacks. Following your suggestions, we have added a paragraph discussing these papers at the end of Section 2:  
"Besides trigger-based backdoor attacks, there are studies on *triggerless* data poisoning attacks, in
which the attacker poisons training data to make the trained model misclassify an individual clean
image or class. A practical approach is treating it as a bilevel optimization problem (Huang et al.,
2020; Geiping et al., 2020), which simulates the training procedure and searches for optimal poi-
soned data directly. The corresponding defenses either pre-filter data with outlier detection Paudice
et al. (2018), detect poisoned data near the target class’s distribution Peri et al. (2020), or utilize
strong augmentations Borgnia et al. (2021). While this line of research is irrelevant to backdoor
attacks, it shares an idea of treating data poisoning as a bilevel optimization with our method. We
solve that problem with alternated learning, as will be discussed in the next section."  
We also added an experiment with data augmentation defense (Borgnia et al. (2021)) in Section A7.7. The results show that our attack is still effective with strong data augmentations.  
### 2. Why we did not compare our attack with [6]:  
We actually compared COMBAT with SleeperAgent and Narcissus, which are recent and released after [6]. Also, [6] attacks via model fine-tuning, while COMBAT and other clean-label attacks target from-scratch model training. Still, we have added a few sentences describing [6] and SleeperAgent in Section 2.2 of our revised paper.  
### 3. Explanation for our experimental setup:  
Our experimental setup is diverse, and we have shown that our attack is effective with different settings. We do not encounter many weaknesses pointed out in [9]: 
- Training with SGD and data augmentation is harder to poison: our victim models are trained with SGD, and we do include data augmentation in the training process.  
- Victim architecture matters: we showed our attack results with different victim architectures in our paper (Section 4.3), and all of them were highly effective.  
- "Clean" attacks are sometimes dirty: some clean-label attacks might increase the trigger strength to favor the attacks; however, our method achieves high performance with $\ell_\infty$ of the trigger is only 10/255  
- Attacks are highly specific to the target image: our attack is also successful in the multi-target setting (Sec A.9 in the revised Appendix), implying that this method is not sensitive to the target label. 
### 4. More examples of poisoned images:  
We have added extra examples in Section A.4 of the revised Appendix.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Designing effective clean-label attacks in backdoor attacks is a challenging task. In this paper, the authors propose a novel clean-label attack mechanism. It allows for different backdoor trigger types and behaviors for single or multiple target labels.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The author proposes a new clean-label attack mechanism called COMBAT.
2. The experimental results show that the proposed method is effective.

Weakness
1. In the introduction, the author clearly points out that "a naive adaptation to clean-label style for BadNets, a common dirty-label method, completely fails." However, most of the experiments were compared to BadNets, which puzzled me.
2. Why did the author design Equation 8? If only to resist the defenses in [1], I think this is too trivial. Please clarify.
3. What is the significance of Figure 1? It is well established that backdoor attacks can change the decision boundaries of the deep neural network. Please clarify more carefully.
4. Does COMBAT work on datasets with large image sizes, such as ImageNet? Please clarify.
5. Figure 2 (d) should show the Grad-CAM of corresponding clean samples.
6. As stated in the abstract, "Our backdoor attacks can reach near-perfect attack success rates and bypass all-state-of-art backdoor defenses." The authors need to do more defense experiments, such as ANP [2], ABL [3], I-BAU[4] etc.
7. As stated in the abstract, “Our proposed mechanism is flexible and customizable, allowing different backdoor trigger types and behaviors for either single or multiple target labels.” What is the empirical support for this statement? Please clarify.

[1] Zeng, Yi, et al. "Rethinking the backdoor attacks' triggers: A frequency perspective." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.
[2] Wu, Dongxian, and Yisen Wang. "Adversarial neuron pruning purifies backdoored deep models." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 16913-16925.
[3] Li, Yige, et al. "Anti-backdoor learning: Training clean models on poisoned data." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 14900-14912.
[4] Zeng, Yi, et al. "Adversarial unlearning of backdoors via implicit hypergradient." arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.03735 (2021).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The methods section is very general, and I hope the author can explain the motivation of COMBAT.
content.summary_of_the_review: It's a good thing to be able to come up with a new paradigm of clean-label attack. However, the proposed method and experimental results did not convince me.

content.title: Thank you for your review, here is our response.
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed review. We would address your concerns as following:  
### 1. Most of the experiments were compared to BadNets:  
Thank you for raising this question. In Table 2, we examine BadNet's performance to confirm further the statement about its failure on clean-label attack settings. Besides, we mainly compared our method with other clean-label backdoor methods. In the GradCAM visualization in Fig. 2d and sample backdoor images in Fig. 4, we include BadNets to emphasize the difference in behavior between COMBAT and other attacks without considering their efficiency. We choose BadNets in these analyses since it is the first and most common attack.  
### 2. Why we designed Equation 8:
We designed this equation to resist frequency defenses like in [1]. Without this proposed regularization, our attack still can bypass all other defenses, but it shows detectable high-frequency artifacts in the frequency spectrum. Hence, such adaptive regularization is needed to make our attack completely stealthy. Despite being simple, this regularization is quite effective, as shown in Sec. 4.4.  
### 3. More explanation about Figure 1:  
The backdoor attack can indeed change the decision boundary of DNN. In our figure, the poisoned training data (red circles) pushes the decision boundary closer to the blue squares, thus reducing the required trigger's strength to make the attack succeed. The decision boundary, in turn, also requires the magnitude of the added signal to be sufficiently large so that poisoned data from non-target class can be misclassified. For example, in Figure 1, if $\eta$ is small, the red circles (poisoned data) are close to the blue circles (clean data), then the decision boundary stays close to the original boundary, and many poisoned test data (red squares) fail to pass this boundary, leading to a lower backdoor success rate. Hence, decision boundary and trigger magnitude depend on each other; we need to optimize both decision boundary and trigger magnitude. We argue in Figure 1 that the "right" poisoned data could further reduce the required trigger magnitude. Experiment results comparing our method and Narcissus confirm that the Narcissus needs a larger backdoor signal since it does not effectively exploit the poisoned data to adjust the decision boundary.  
### 4. COMBAT performance on large image sizes dataset:  
COMBAT can work on datasets with large image sizes. We have added an experiment on ImageNet to our revised paper (Section A.10 in the Appendix) to demonstrate this ability. Specifically, we randomly select 10 classes for training and testing due to time and resource limits. We keep the input resolution 224x224 and use PreReactResNet 18 as the classifier's backbone. We employ $\eta=10/255$ and the poisoning rate \rho=5% and acquire ASR 95.20\%, confirming COMBAT's efficiency on large-image datasets.  
### 5. Grad-CAM of corresponding clean samples:  
Thanks for your usefule suggestion. We have added the Grad-CAM visualization on clean samples in our revised paper.  
### 6. More defenses experiments:  
Thanks for your suggestion. We already provided an experiment with the I-BAU defense in Section A.5.4 (or A.7.4 in the revised version) of the Appendix. As reported, on both CIFAR10 and GTSRB, the ASR of the victim models remains higher than 90\% in most of the tests, and it never drops to under 70\%, indicating that I-BAU is not robust against COMBAT. 
We have also added experiments with ANP and ABL to Section A.7.5 and A.7.8 of the revised Appendix. In both experiments, the defenses cannot break our attack.  
### 7. Empirical support for the aforementioned statement:  
We already supported that claim in our submission pre-rebuttal. First, we demonstrate that COMBAT can work on warping-based triggers (a different backdoor trigger type) in Section 5. Next, we show that COMBAT can support Imperceptible and Input-aware backdoor triggers (different behaviors) in Section A.6 of the Appendix. Finally, we examine COMBAT in the case of multiple target labels, also in Section A.6 of the Appendix.  
### 8. Explanation for the motivation of COMBAT:  
We provide the motivation of our COMBAT design in the section of each proposal. Specifically, in Section 3.2, we explain the reason to use Trigger Generator as "Note that we use image-dependent trigger instead of a fixed, global one like in most of previous works. It is more flexible and allows to define extra properties like input-awareness". In Section 3.3, we provide the reason of using alternated training in the first paragraph.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies backdoor attacks—attacks where an adversary injects “poisoned” data into a training dataset, in order to cause the resulting model to associate an input “trigger” pattern with a specific output. Specifically, the authors focus on “clean-label” attacks, where the goal is to only inject inputs that would appear consistent with their labels to a human.

The authors propose learning a model to apply the trigger to each individual input. This model will be trained in parallel to a standard model that is meant to approximate the victim model being poisoned (in an alternating fashion). The authors find that their attack outperforms existing clean-label methods, while also working in a transfer setting (where the surrogate model used to train the trigger-applying model differs from the model being attacked).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- The idea of learning a model to produce the backdoor trigger has been explored before, but, to the best of my knowledge, this is the first work that does so in the clean-label regime.
- The attack does appear to be effective, significantly outperforming other clean-label methods.
- The authors evaluate a number of existing defenses.

Weaknesses

- The fact that each trigger is input-dependent and produced by a model makes it hard to reason about how the attack works. Specifically, for any fixed, non-poisoned model, one could construct adversarial examples with the same perturbation budget, call them “backdoor triggers” and achieve 100% ASR. While this is not necessarily what is happening here, the authors would need to argue further and/or provide experimental support to show that poisoning is a meaningful component of the attack. In fact, the existing ablations (Fig 3) show that (a) alternating training does not always significantly outperform training the trigger using a clean surrogate model, (b) the attack is successful with as few as 10 (?) poisoned images. At the very least, one would expect an experiment that measures how well the attack works when learned with a fixed, clean surrogate model and 0 poisoned images (effectively simulating a learned adversarial perturbation).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: I did not have trouble reading the paper.

Quality: The results are interesting, but additional analysis is needed to support the paper.

Novelty: To the best of my knowledge, this is the first time that learned backdoor triggers are applied in the clean-label setting (although they have been developed in the standard setting).

Reproducibility: The authors provide a description of their method as well as code as part of the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while the approach is interesting and potentially powerful, additional analysis is necessary to understand whether the method actually succeeds by poisoning the training dataset or by finding perturbations that fool the resulting model at test-time.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments. We would address your concerns below:  
### 1. Poisoning is a meaningful component of the attack:  
Thanks for your interesting concern. We have added Section A.5 to our revised Appendix discussing this concern. Specifically, we ran experiments w/ and w/o data poisoning, using $\rho$ = 5\% and $\eta$ = 10/255, and reported the results in Table 6 on all datasets. We admit that even without data poisoning, the ASRs looked quite good, but they were far from 100%. The ASRs improved significantly and approached 100% when data was poisoned during the training process, implying that data poisoning played an important role in the success of our attack.   
### 2. Alternated training outperforms training the trigger using a clean surrogate model:  
We have further investigated the role of alternated training by running experiments w/ and w/o alternated training on more datasets and we have added Section A.6 to show the results. As shown in Fig. 5, the models w/ alternated training constantly outperform the models w/o using it.

content.title: Appreciate the additional experiments, but they reaffirm my concerns
content.comment:
I appreciate the authors' effort in providing additional experiments.

Unfortunately, these additional results reinforce my concerns... The main claim of the paper is that alternating training leads to near-perfect backdoor attacks. According to the abstract "The key component is a trigger pattern generator, which is trained together with a surrogate model in an alternate manner." However, as shown by the additional experiments (and the original non-alternating ablation):
- The trigger generator alone can function as a powerful adversarial examples generator. It achieves 90% attack success rate without injecting any poisoned examples! Thus the effect of the poisoning component of the attack is smaller than the effect of perturbations generated.
- The effect of alternating training, especially in the regime where the attack achieves "near-perfect" success is relatively small. Even though alternating training consistently outperforms the non-alternating variant, the marginal difference is not particularly large.

Overall, I still believe that this in an interesting finding in the space of adversarial ML, however, these are important caveats that need to be incorporated into the paper's narrative. Thus, I cannot change my score at the time.
